decks.title: Areas Related to Circles — Part 1: Sectors and arcs
goals: Recognise sectors, arcs, minor and major parts of a circle
Find the area of a sector and the length of its arc for any angle
Find the perimeter of a sector
Work backwards from an arc or an area to the angle or radius
Solve clock, pendulum and sports-ground problems

slides.heading: Areas Related to Circles, Part 1: Sectors and arcs
slides.body_md: A slice of a circle is just a **fraction** of the whole.

slides.narration: Welcome to Areas Related to Circles. Think of a slice of pizza, the part of a cricket ground between two fielders, or the area a wiper or a sprinkler covers. Each is a slice of a circle called a sector. The big idea of this part is simple: a sector is a fraction of the whole circle, and the angle tells you which fraction.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find the **length of an arc** and the perimeter of a sector
Work backwards to an angle or a radius
Use the value of $\pi$ the question gives
slides.narration: These are your goals for part one. You already know that a circle of radius r has area pi r squared and circumference two pi r. Everything today comes from those two formulas and one fraction.

slides.heading: Parts of a circle
slides.body_md: Two radii cut a circle into a **minor sector** and a **major sector**; their arcs are the minor and major arcs. The two angles at the centre add up to $360^\circ$.

visual.spec: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 248" role="img" aria-label="A circle with two radii dividing it into a shaded minor sector, with the highlighted minor arc, and an unshaded major sector bounded by the major arc." font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="none"><title>A circle with two radii dividing it into a shaded minor sector, with the highlighted minor arc, and an unshaded major sector bounded by the major arc.</title><path d="M 140 128 L 223.14 80 A 96 96 0 0 0 92 44.86 Z" fill="var(--diagram-fill)" stroke="none" stroke-width="1.6"/><circle cx="140" cy="128" r="96" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="140" y1="128" x2="223.14" y2="80" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="140" y1="128" x2="92" y2="44.86" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M 223.14 80 A 96 96 0 0 0 92 44.86" fill="none" stroke="var(--diagram-accent)" stroke-width="3"/><circle cx="140" cy="128" r="2.8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="130" y="138" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13">O</text><text x="153.46" y="77.77" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">minor sector</text><text x="127.58" y="174.36" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">major sector</text><text x="168.47" y="21.75" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">minor arc</text><text x="195" y="223.26" fill="var(--diagram-muted)" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">major arc</text></svg>
visual.alt: A circle with two radii dividing it into a shaded minor sector, with the highlighted minor arc, and an unshaded major sector bounded by the major arc.
visual.caption: Minor sector (shaded) and major sector: their angles add up to $360^\circ$.

slides.narration: Two radii split a circle into two sectors. The smaller one is the minor sector, and its curved edge is the minor arc. The rest is the major sector, with the major arc. If the minor sector has angle theta, the major sector has three hundred and sixty minus theta degrees. Unless a question says major, sector means the minor one.

slides.heading: The fraction idea
slides.body_md: A full turn of $360^\circ$ gives the whole circle, so an angle $\theta$ gives the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the area **and** of the circumference.

visual.alt: Table: a full turn gives the whole area pi r squared and the whole circumference 2 pi r; a half turn gives half of each; a quarter turn a quarter of each; an angle theta gives the fraction theta over 360 of each.
visual.caption: A sector is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circle.

slides.narration: Look at the table. Half a turn gives half the circle, a quarter turn gives a quarter. So an angle theta gives theta over three sixty of the circle. Multiply that fraction by pi r squared for the area, or by two pi r for the length of the arc. These are the two formulas of the chapter; there is nothing new to memorise.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: area, arc and perimeter
slides.body_md: A sector has radius $21$ cm and angle $60^\circ$. Find its area, its arc length and its perimeter. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)

visual.alt: A sector OAB with radius 21 centimetres and an angle of 60 degrees at the centre O. Its arc AB is one sixth of the full circle.
visual.caption: Sector of radius $21$ cm and angle $60^\circ$: one-sixth of the circle.

slides.narration: Find the fraction first: sixty out of three sixty is one sixth. Then take one sixth of the whole area, one thousand three hundred and eighty six, which gives two hundred and thirty one square centimetres. The arc is one sixth of the circumference, twenty two centimetres. For the perimeter, do not forget the two radii.

slides.heading: Quick check: area of a sector
slides.body_md: Find the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ first.
slides.narration: What fraction of a full turn is forty five degrees? Take that fraction of the area of the whole circle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a cricket boundary
slides.body_md: A cricket ground in Chennai is a circle of radius $70$ m. Two fielders stand on the boundary so that the angle between them at the pitch is $45^\circ$. Find the length of boundary rope between them and the area of ground they guard. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)

slides.narration: The angle between the two fielders is one eighth of a full turn. So the rope between them is one eighth of the boundary, fifty five metres, and the region they guard is one eighth of the ground. The check uses a neat shortcut: the area of a sector is half the arc times the radius, just like a triangle.

slides.heading: A shortcut: area $= \dfrac12 \times$ arc $\times$ radius
slides.body_md: Since $\dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2 = \dfrac12 r \times \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$:
bullets: Useful when the **arc length** is given and the angle is not
A sector behaves like a "triangle" with base $l$ and height $r$

visual.alt: Table of three sectors: arc 22 and radius 21 give area 231; arc 55 and radius 70 give area 1925; arc 44 and radius 35 give area 770.
visual.caption: No angle needed.

slides.narration: Here is a shortcut worth remembering. The area of a sector equals half the arc length times the radius. Picture the sector as a very thin triangle with base equal to the arc and height equal to the radius. When a question gives the arc and the radius but not the angle, this saves a step.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a swinging pendulum
slides.body_md: A pendulum $35$ cm long swings so that its bob moves along an arc of $22$ cm. Through what angle does it swing? (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)
bullets: **Step 1 —** The bob moves on a circle of radius $35$ cm: circumference $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220$ cm.

slides.narration: Work backwards. The arc is a fraction of the full circumference, and that same fraction is theta over three sixty. The circumference of a circle of radius thirty five is two hundred and twenty, so the arc is one tenth of it. One tenth of three sixty is thirty six degrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: perimeter of a sector
slides.body_md: Perimeter means the whole boundary.
slides.narration: Find the arc first. Then ask yourself: how many straight edges does a sector have, and how long is each?

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a major sector
slides.body_md: At a birthday party in Patna, a quarter of a round cake of radius $14$ cm is eaten. Find the area of the top of the remaining cake and the length of its curved edge. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)
bullets: **Step 1 —** The remaining part is a major sector of angle $360^\circ - 90^\circ = 270^\circ$.

visual.spec: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 256 256" role="img" aria-label="A circle of radius 14 centimetres with a quarter (the minor sector of 90 degrees) left white and the remaining major sector of 270 degrees shaded." font-family="sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="none"><title>A circle of radius 14 centimetres with a quarter (the minor sector of 90 degrees) left white and the remaining major sector of 270 degrees shaded.</title><path d="M 128 128 L 128 32 A 96 96 0 1 0 224 128 Z" fill="var(--diagram-fill)" stroke="none" stroke-width="1.6"/><circle cx="128" cy="128" r="96" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="128" y1="128" x2="224" y2="128" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="128" y1="128" x2="128" y2="32" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M 224 128 A 96 96 0 0 0 128 32" fill="none" stroke="var(--diagram-accent)" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M 148 128 A 20 20 0 0 0 128 108" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.1"/><circle cx="128" cy="128" r="2.8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="118" y="138" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13">O</text><text x="236" y="128" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13">A</text><text x="128" y="20" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="13">B</text><text x="152.04" y="103.96" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">90°</text><text x="175.41" y="135.51" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle" font-size="12">14 cm</text></svg>
visual.alt: A circle of radius 14 centimetres with a quarter (the minor sector of 90 degrees) left white and the remaining major sector of 270 degrees shaded.
visual.caption: Major sector $=$ circle $-$ minor sector: angle $270^\circ$.

slides.narration: The eaten piece is a quadrant, so what is left is a major sector of two hundred and seventy degrees. You can use the fraction three quarters directly, or subtract the quadrant from the whole circle. Both give four hundred and sixty two square centimetres. Doing it both ways is a good habit in exams.

slides.heading: Angles from clocks and the value of pi
slides.body_md: Many problems hide the angle: find it first. And always use the value of $\pi$ the question states.

visual.alt: Table of clock hands: the minute hand turns 6 degrees per minute, 120 degrees in 20 minutes; the hour hand turns half a degree per minute, 10 degrees in 20 minutes; the seconds hand makes a full turn every minute.
visual.caption: Find the angle first, then use the sector formulas.

slides.narration: Clock problems are really sector problems in disguise. The minute hand turns six degrees every minute, and the hour hand half a degree. Once you know the angle, use the usual formulas. Also read the question for the value of pi. Twenty two by seven suits radii like seven or twenty one; three point one four suits radii like ten.

slides.heading: Choosing the value of $\pi$
slides.body_md: Different values of $\pi$ give slightly different answers; the marking scheme expects the one in the question.

rows: leave the answer in terms of $\pi$

visual.alt: Table: when the question says pi equals 22 over 7, cancel the 7 with radii such as 7, 14, 21 or 10.5; when it says 3.14, work in decimals; if nothing is said, leave the answer in terms of pi.
visual.caption: Always use the value of $\pi$ the question gives.

slides.narration: If the question says twenty two by seven, use it, and look for sevens to cancel. If it says three point one four, work in decimals. If it gives no value, leave pi in the answer, like six pi square centimetres. Using a different value from the one given can cost you the final mark.

slides.heading: Quick check: from arc to angle
slides.body_md: Compare the arc with the whole circumference.
slides.narration: What is the full circumference of this circle? What fraction of it is the given arc?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Area $= \dfrac12 lr$ when the arc is known
Major sector: angle $360^\circ - \theta$, or circle $-$ minor

visual.alt: Summary table: sector area is theta over 360 times pi r squared; arc length is theta over 360 times 2 pi r; the perimeter of a sector is the arc plus two radii; the area is also half the arc times the radius; a major sector is the circle minus the minor sector.
visual.caption: Five formulas for part one.

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A sector is a fraction of the circle, theta over three sixty. Use it with pi r squared for area and with two pi r for arc length. Add two radii for the perimeter. Work backwards from an arc or an area to find the angle, and use the major angle, three sixty minus theta, for major sectors.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Sector area / arc (2 marks):** correct formula with $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ 1 + answer with unit 1
**Mistake:** using $2\pi r$ for area or $\pi r^2$ for arc length
**Mistake:** forgetting the two radii in a perimeter
**Mistake:** units: cm for lengths, cm² for areas
slides.narration: Write the formula first, with theta over three sixty; that line earns a mark even if the arithmetic slips. Check your units: lengths in centimetres, areas in square centimetres. A quick sense check helps: a sector of sixty degrees must be one sixth of the circle. And for perimeter, include both radii.

decks.title: Areas Related to Circles — Part 2: Segments and shaded regions
goals: Find the area of a minor segment for central angles of 60°, 90° and 120°
Find the area of a major segment
Find areas of shaded regions made of sectors, segments, triangles and squares
Find perimeters of segments and shaded regions

slides.heading: Areas Related to Circles, Part 2: Segments and shaded regions
slides.body_md: Cut a circle with a chord and you get two **segments**.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. A straight chord cuts a circle into two pieces called segments. The arched glass above an old doorway is one. In this part we find the areas of segments, and then the areas of shaded designs made from circles, squares and triangles, like tiles, flower beds and rangoli patterns.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Find a **minor segment** as sector minus triangle
Find perimeters made of arcs and straight lines
slides.narration: Here are the goals. For segments, the syllabus uses only three central angles: sixty, ninety and one hundred and twenty degrees. Shaded-region questions combine simple shapes; the skill is to plan which pieces to add and which to subtract.

slides.heading: Segment = sector − triangle
slides.body_md: The sector $OAB$ is made of $\triangle OAB$ and the minor segment. So

math: \text{Minor segment} = \text{sector } OAB - \triangle OAB, \qquad \text{Major segment} = \pi r^2 - \text{minor segment}
slides.narration: Look at the sector O A B. Draw the chord A B, and the sector splits into two parts: the triangle O A B and the segment. So the segment is the sector minus the triangle. The major segment is everything else in the circle: the circle minus the minor segment.

slides.heading: The triangle for each syllabus angle
slides.body_md: The area of $\triangle OAB$ (two sides $r$) depends on the angle at $O$:

visual.alt: Table of the three syllabus angles: for 60 degrees the triangle is equilateral with area root 3 over 4 r squared; for 90 degrees it is right isosceles with area half r squared; for 120 degrees it has height r over 2 and base root 3 r, area root 3 over 4 r squared. The segment is the sector minus the triangle.
visual.caption: The syllabus uses only these three angles for segments.

slides.narration: You need the area of the triangle O A B. At ninety degrees it is a right triangle with legs r and r, so its area is half r squared. At sixty degrees it is equilateral, so use root three over four r squared. At one hundred and twenty degrees, drop a perpendicular from O: its height is r over two and the base is root three r, giving the same root three over four r squared.

slides.body_md: A chord of a circle of radius $14$ cm subtends a right angle at the centre. Find the areas of the minor and major segments. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)

slides.body_md: Sector, triangle, subtract.
slides.narration: Find the sector of ninety degrees, then the right triangle. Which of the options is their difference?

slides.body_md: A chord of a circle of radius $12$ cm subtends $60^\circ$ at the centre. Find the area of the minor segment. (Use $\pi = 3.14$, $\sqrt3 = 1.73$.)

slides.narration: With sixty degrees, the two radii and the chord form an equilateral triangle, because the base angles must also be sixty. So use root three over four times r squared. Here the segment is quite thin, only about thirteen square centimetres, which matches the picture. Use the decimal values the question gives.

bullets: **Step 2 —** $OM \perp AB$: $OM = 15$ cm, $AB = 30\sqrt3$ cm, so $\triangle OAB = \dfrac12 \times 30\sqrt3 \times 15 = 225\sqrt3 = 389.25$ cm².

slides.narration: For one hundred and twenty degrees, drop the perpendicular O M to the chord. It bisects the angle, so each half is sixty degrees, and O M is half the radius, fifteen. Half the chord is fifteen root three, so the chord is thirty root three. The triangle has area two hundred and twenty five root three, about three hundred and eighty nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: a 60° segment
slides.body_md: Equilateral triangle for $60^\circ$.
slides.narration: Which formula gives the area of an equilateral triangle of side six? Subtract it from the sector.

slides.heading: Planning a shaded region
slides.body_md: Shaded-region questions combine **simple** shapes. Plan before you calculate.

nodes.label: Compute each area with the given $\pi$

visual.alt: Strategy chart for shaded regions: name the whole figure, list the pieces added or removed, check for overlaps, compute each area with the given value of pi, and add or subtract.
visual.caption: Every shaded-region question is "whole plus or minus pieces".

slides.narration: Here is a plan for any shaded region. Name the whole figure. List the pieces cut out or added. Check whether pieces overlap, so nothing is counted twice. Then compute each area with the value of pi given, and finally add or subtract. Write the plan in one line at the start of your answer; examiners give credit for it.

slides.body_md: A square tile of side $28$ cm has a quadrant of radius $7$ cm cut at each corner and a circle of radius $7$ cm cut at the centre. Find the area of the shaded part. (Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.)
bullets: **Step 2 —** Four quadrants of radius $7$ make one circle: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ cm².

slides.heading: Quick check: corners of a square
slides.body_md: Four equal quadrants make one circle.
slides.narration: What do the four corner pieces add up to? Subtract that from the square.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: sectors in a triangle

bullets: **Step 2 —** Each sector has angle $60^\circ$; three of them make $180^\circ$, a semicircle: $\dfrac12 \times 3.14 \times 100 = 157$ cm².
**Note —** The sectors just meet at the midpoints of the sides, so they do not overlap.

slides.body_md: **Perimeter of a segment** $=$ arc $+$ chord. For any shaded region, walk round its boundary and add each straight piece and each arc.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Shaded region $=$ whole $\pm$ pieces; four equal quadrants $=$ one circle
Perimeter of a segment $=$ arc $+$ chord

visual.alt: Summary table: a minor segment is the sector minus the triangle; a major segment is the circle minus the minor segment; a ring is pi times R squared minus r squared; a shaded region is the whole plus or minus its pieces; the perimeter of a segment is arc plus chord.
visual.caption: Every answer is built from sectors, triangles and squares.

slides.narration: To sum up part two. A segment is a sector minus a triangle, and you only need three triangle formulas. A major segment is the circle minus the minor one. For shaded regions, plan whole plus or minus pieces, look for quarter circles that join into a full circle, and walk round the boundary for perimeters.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **Segment (3 marks):** sector 1 + triangle 1 + subtraction with unit 1
**Shaded region (3–5 marks):** plan 1 + each piece 1 + final answer 1
**Mistake:** subtracting the triangle again for a major segment
**Mistake:** rounding early: keep exact values until the end
slides.narration: In segment questions, show the sector and the triangle on separate lines; each earns a mark. Use the right triangle formula for the angle. In shaded regions, write your plan first, and keep unrounded values until the last step so that your final answer matches the scheme. Finally, give the unit, square centimetres or square metres.

notes.title: Areas Related to Circles — chapter notes

sections.heading: 1. Circle facts and the value of π
sections.body_md:
For a circle of radius $r$: area $= \pi r^2$, circumference $= 2\pi r$.

Use the value of $\pi$ given in the question: $\dfrac{22}{7}$ (choose radii that cancel the $7$) or $3.14$; if none is given, leave $\pi$ in the answer.

A **ring** between concentric circles of radii $R > r$ has area $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$ — not $\pi(R - r)^2$. A wheel covers one circumference per revolution.

key_terms.definition_md: The region between two concentric circles.

rows: leave the answer in terms of $\pi$

visual.alt: Table: when the question says pi equals 22 over 7, cancel the 7 with radii such as 7, 14, 21 or 10.5; when it says 3.14, work in decimals; if nothing is said, leave the answer in terms of pi.
visual.caption: Always use the value of $\pi$ the question gives.

sections.heading: 2. Sectors and arcs
sections.body_md:
Two radii divide a circle into a **minor sector** (angle $\theta$) and a **major sector** (angle $360^\circ - \theta$). A sector of angle $\theta$ is the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of the circle, so

$$\text{Area} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2, \qquad \text{Arc length } l = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r.$$

Perimeter of a sector $= l + 2r$. Also $\text{Area} = \dfrac12 lr$.

*Example:* $r = 21$ cm, $\theta = 60^\circ$: area $231$ cm², arc $22$ cm, perimeter $64$ cm.

key_terms.definition_md: The region between two radii and the arc between them.

sections.heading: 3. Finding the angle first; working backwards
sections.body_md:
Many problems hide the angle:
- **Clocks:** minute hand $6^\circ$ per minute; hour hand $0.5^\circ$ per minute.
- **Equal slices:** $n$ equal sectors have angle $\dfrac{360^\circ}{n}$ (a $24$-spoke wheel: $15^\circ$).
- **Fractions:** a sector that is $\dfrac15$ of the circle has angle $72^\circ$.

**Backwards:** from an arc, $\dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac{l}{2\pi r}$ (pendulum $35$ cm, arc $22$ cm gives $36^\circ$); from an area, $\dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac{A}{\pi r^2}$.

For the same angle, sector areas are in the ratio of $r^2$ and arcs in the ratio of $r$.

sections.heading: 4. Segments
sections.body_md:
A chord divides a circle into a **minor segment** and a **major segment**.

$$\text{Minor segment} = \text{sector } OAB - \triangle OAB, \qquad \text{Major segment} = \pi r^2 - \text{minor segment}.$$

The syllabus uses central angles of $60^\circ$, $90^\circ$ and $120^\circ$:
- $90^\circ$: $\triangle OAB = \dfrac12 r^2$.
- $60^\circ$: $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral, area $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2$.
- $120^\circ$: drop $OM \perp AB$; $OM = \dfrac r2$, $AB = \sqrt3\,r$, area $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{4}r^2$.

Perimeter of a segment $=$ arc $+$ chord ($90^\circ$: chord $= r\sqrt2$; $60^\circ$: chord $= r$; $120^\circ$: chord $= r\sqrt3$).

sections.heading: 5. Shaded regions
sections.body_md:
Plan: **whole $\pm$ pieces**, checking overlaps.

Useful facts:
- Four equal quadrants at the corners of a square make one full circle.
- The three corner sectors (equal radius) of any triangle make a semicircle, since the angles add to $180^\circ$.
- A leaf between two quadrants on a square's diagonal $=$ two $90^\circ$ segments $=$ quadrant $+$ quadrant $-$ square.
- The region inside a circle but outside an inscribed square is four $90^\circ$ segments.

*Examples:* tile $28$ cm with corner quadrants and a central circle, radius $7$: $784 - 154 - 154 = 476$ cm². Equilateral triangle side $20$ with corner sectors of radius $10$: $173 - 157 = 16$ cm².

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *Sector / arc (2 marks):* formula with $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ 1; answer with unit 1.
- *Segment (3 marks):* sector 1; triangle 1; difference 1.
- *Shaded region (3–5 marks):* plan 1; each component 1; final answer 1.

**Common mistakes**
1. $2\pi r$ in an area, or $\pi r^2$ in an arc.
2. Forgetting the two radii in the perimeter of a sector (or adding radii to a segment's perimeter).
3. $\dfrac12 r^2$ used for a $60^\circ$ or $120^\circ$ triangle.
4. $\pi(R - r)^2$ for a ring.
5. A different value of $\pi$ from the one given; rounding too early.
6. Missing units: cm for lengths, cm² for areas.

questions.stem_md: The area of a sector of angle $\theta$ (in degrees) of a circle of radius $r$ is
questions.solution_md: A full turn of $360^\circ$ gives the whole area $\pi r^2$, so an angle $\theta$ gives the fraction $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of it. Option (b) is the arc length.

questions.stem_md: The length of the arc of a sector of angle $90^\circ$ of a circle of radius $14$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $l = \dfrac{90}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = \dfrac14 \times 88 = 22$ cm. Option (c) uses $\dfrac12$ of the circumference; (d) is the area of the sector in cm².

questions.stem_md: The area of a sector of angle $45^\circ$ of a circle of radius $28$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{45}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 \times 28 = \dfrac18 \times 2464 = 308$ cm². Option (d) uses $\dfrac14$ instead of $\dfrac18$; (a) is the arc length.

questions.stem_md: The perimeter of a sector of angle $120^\circ$ of a circle of radius $10.5$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Arc $= \dfrac{120}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10.5 = \dfrac13 \times 66 = 22$ cm.

**Step 2.** Perimeter $= $ arc $+ 2r = 22 + 21 = 43$ cm.

Option (a) forgets the two radii; (b) adds only one radius; (c) is the area in cm².

questions.stem_md: The angle turned by the minute hand of a clock in 20 minutes is
questions.solution_md: The minute hand turns $360^\circ$ in $60$ minutes, i.e. $6^\circ$ per minute. In $20$ minutes: $20 \times 6 = 120^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: A sector of a circle of radius $r$ has arc length $l$. Its area is
questions.solution_md: Area $= \dfrac{\theta}{360}\pi r^2 = \dfrac12 r \times \left(\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r\right) = \dfrac12 lr$ — like a triangle with base $l$ and height $r$.

questions.stem_md: The area of a sector is one-fifth of the area of its circle. The angle of the sector is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{\theta}{360} = \dfrac15$, so $\theta = 72^\circ$.

questions.stem_md: Two sectors have the same central angle, in circles of radii 3 cm and 6 cm. The ratio of their areas is
questions.solution_md: For the same angle, area $\propto r^2$: $3^2 : 6^2 = 9 : 36 = 1 : 4$. Option (a) is the ratio of the arc lengths.

questions.stem_md: The area of a circle is $154$ cm². The area of a sector of this circle with angle $72^\circ$ is
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{72}{360} \times 154 = \dfrac15 \times 154 = 30.8$ cm².

questions.stem_md: A chord of a circle of radius $14$ cm subtends a right angle at the centre. The area of the minor segment is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Sector $= \dfrac14 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 196 = 154$ cm².

**Step 2.** $\triangle OAB = \dfrac12 \times 14 \times 14 = 98$ cm².

**Step 3.** Segment $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm². Option (c) is the sector, (d) the triangle, (a) the major segment.

questions.stem_md: The area of the minor segment of a circle of radius $r$ cut off by a chord that subtends $90^\circ$ at the centre is
questions.solution_md: Sector $\dfrac{\pi r^2}{4}$ minus right triangle $\dfrac12 r^2$. Option (b) uses the triangle for $60^\circ$; (a) forgets the triangle.

questions.stem_md: A chord $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $10$ cm subtends $60^\circ$ at $O$. The area of $\triangle OAB$ is
questions.solution_md: $OA = OB$ and $\angle AOB = 60^\circ$, so $\triangle OAB$ is equilateral with side $10$ cm: area $= \dfrac{\sqrt3}{4} \times 10^2 = 25\sqrt3$ cm². Option (a) uses the right-triangle formula $\dfrac12 r^2$.

questions.stem_md: In a circle of radius $14$ cm, the minor segment cut off by a chord has area $56$ cm². The area of the major segment is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: Circle $= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14 = 616$ cm². Major segment $= 616 - 56 = 560$ cm². Option (c) adds instead of subtracting; (d) is the major sector of a $90^\circ$ chord, which still contains the triangle.

questions.stem_md: A square is inscribed in a circle of radius $7$ cm. The area of the region inside the circle but outside the square is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: The diagonal of the square is the diameter, $14$ cm, so its area is $\dfrac12 \times 14^2 = 98$ cm². Circle $= 154$ cm². Region $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm² (four $90^\circ$ segments). Option (c) wrongly takes the side of the square as $7$ cm.

questions.stem_md: The area of the ring between two concentric circles of radii $14$ cm and $7$ cm is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: $\pi(R^2 - r^2) = \dfrac{22}{7}(196 - 49) = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 147 = 462$ cm². Option (d) uses $\pi(R - r)^2$; (b) adds the areas.

questions.stem_md: From each corner of a square sheet of side $14$ cm, a quadrant of radius $7$ cm is cut off. The area of the remaining sheet is (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: The four quadrants together make one circle of radius $7$ cm: $154$ cm². Remaining $= 196 - 154 = 42$ cm².

questions.stem_md: A wheel of radius $35$ cm rolls without slipping. How many complete revolutions does it make in covering $1.1$ km? (use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$)
questions.solution_md: Circumference $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220$ cm. $1.1$ km $= 110000$ cm. Revolutions $= \dfrac{110000}{220} = 500$. Option (c) uses the radius instead of the diameter; (d) forgets to convert km to cm properly.

questions.stem_md: The circumference and the area of a circle are numerically equal. The radius of the circle is
questions.solution_md: $2\pi r = \pi r^2 \Rightarrow r^2 - 2r = 0 \Rightarrow r(r - 2) = 0$, and $r \ne 0$, so $r = 2$ units.

questions.stem_md:
A square park in Lucknow has side $42$ m. At each corner there is a flower bed in the shape of a quadrant of radius $14$ m, and at the centre there is a circular fountain of diameter $14$ m. The rest of the park is lawn.

(a) Find the area of the flower beds.

(b) Find the area of the lawn.

(c) Find the cost of turfing the lawn at ₹$25$ per m².

(d) The lawn is edged with a low hedge along its boundary with the flower beds and along the sides of the park. Find the length of hedge along the four quadrant arcs.
Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Four quadrants of radius $14$ m make one circle: $\dfrac{22}{7} \times 196 = 616$ m².

(b) Fountain $= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154$ m². Lawn $= 42^2 - 616 - 154 = 1764 - 770 = 994$ m².

(c) Cost $= 994 \times 25 = $ ₹$24850$.

questions.stem_md:
A chord $AB$ of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $14$ cm subtends a right angle at $O$.

(a) Find the area of the minor sector.

(b) Find the area of the minor segment.

(c) Find the area of the major segment.

(d) Find the length of the chord and the perimeter of the minor segment.
Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$ and $\sqrt2 = 1.414$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Sector $= \dfrac14 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 196 = 154$ cm².

(b) $\triangle OAB = \dfrac12 \times 14 \times 14 = 98$ cm². Minor segment $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm².

(c) Circle $= 616$ cm². Major segment $= 616 - 56 = 560$ cm².

(d) $AB = \sqrt{14^2 + 14^2} = 14\sqrt2 = 14 \times 1.414 = 19.796$ cm. Minor arc $= \dfrac14 \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 = 22$ cm. Perimeter of the minor segment $= 22 + 19.796 = 41.796 \approx 41.80$ cm.

questions.solution_md: The perimeter of a segment is its arc plus its chord.

A cricket ground in Raipur is a circle of radius $63$ m. The inner fielding circle, with the same centre, has radius $28$ m. The region between the two circles is the outfield.

(a) Find the area of the outfield.

(b) A sector of angle $36^\circ$ at the centre marks the "third man" region. Find the area of the outfield inside this sector.

(c) Find the length of the boundary rope along this sector.

(d) Find the cost of re-turfing the whole outfield at ₹$12$ per m².

answer.model_answer_md:

(b) $\dfrac{36}{360} = \dfrac{1}{10}$ of the outfield: $1001$ m².

(c) Boundary arc $= \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 63 = \dfrac{1}{10} \times 396 = 39.6$ m.

questions.stem_md:
An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle with centre $O$ and radius $10$ cm. The three segments outside the triangle are shaded.

(a) Show that each side of the triangle subtends $120^\circ$ at $O$.

(b) Find the area of one shaded segment.

(c) Find the total shaded area, and check it by subtracting the triangle from the circle.
Use $\pi = 3.14$ and $\sqrt3 = 1.73$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $OA = OB = OC$ and $AB = BC = CA$, so $\triangle OAB \cong \triangle OBC \cong \triangle OCA$ (SSS). Their three equal angles at $O$ add to $360^\circ$, so each is $120^\circ$.

(b) Sector $= \dfrac13 \times 3.14 \times 100 = 104.67$ cm² (exactly $\dfrac{314}{3}$). $\triangle OAB = \dfrac{1.73}{4} \times 100 = 43.25$ cm². Segment $= 104.67 - 43.25 \approx 61.42$ cm².

(c) Shaded $= 3 \times 61.4167 \approx 184.25$ cm².

Check: circle $= 314$ cm²; $\triangle ABC = 3 \times 43.25 = 129.75$ cm²; $314 - 129.75 = 184.25$ cm² ✓.

questions.stem_md:
$OAB$ is a quadrant of a circle with centre $O$ and radius $14$ cm. A semicircle is drawn outside the quadrant on the chord $AB$ as diameter. The crescent-shaped region inside the semicircle but outside the quadrant is shaded.

(a) Find the length of $AB$ and the area of the semicircle.

(b) Find the area of the minor segment of the quadrant on $AB$.

(c) Find the area of the crescent.

(d) Compare the crescent with $\triangle OAB$. What do you notice?
Use $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $AB = \sqrt{14^2 + 14^2} = 14\sqrt2$ cm, so the semicircle has radius $7\sqrt2$ cm and $r^2 = 98$. Its area $= \dfrac12 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 98 = 154$ cm².

(b) Segment $=$ quadrant $-$ triangle $= 154 - 98 = 56$ cm².

(c) The semicircle consists of the crescent and the segment, so crescent $= 154 - 56 = 98$ cm².

(d) $\triangle OAB = \dfrac12 \times 14 \times 14 = 98$ cm². The curved crescent has **exactly** the same area as the straight-sided triangle — and the result does not depend on the value used for $\pi$: crescent $= \dfrac{\pi r^2}{4} - \left(\dfrac{\pi r^2}{4} - \dfrac{r^2}{2}\right) = \dfrac{r^2}{2}$.

questions.solution_md: The semicircle on $AB$ has area $\dfrac12\pi\left(\dfrac{r\sqrt2}{2}\right)^2 = \dfrac{\pi r^2}{4}$, the same as the quadrant.

children.solution_md: The track is the ring between radii $35$ m and $35 - 7 = 28$ m: $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$. Option (b) squares the difference; (d) uses the width as the inner radius.

children.stem_md: Find the area of the track in m².
**(i)** Find the cost of paving the track at ₹50 per m².

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** How much longer is the outer edge of the track than its inner edge?

answer.model_answer_md: Outer $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220$ m; inner $= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 176$ m. Difference $= 44$ m (always $2\pi \times$ width).
